title: The 2010 Perseids over the VLT
caption: A bright Perseid meteor over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A bright meteor streaks over the platform of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal. Reddish light from the Moon, setting just beyond the left edge of the frame, illuminates the scene. This shot, from the night of 13–14 August 2010, was hand-picked from 8000 exposures by ESO Photo Ambassador Stéphane Guisard, who ran three cameras taking time-lapse pictures over two nights.

The meteor belongs to the Perseid shower, which peaks every year in mid-August as Earth passes through debris left by Comet Swift-Tuttle. Most of the particles are smaller than a grain of sand and burn up in the atmosphere, leaving glowing trails.

The Perseids are best seen from the northern hemisphere, but Paranal's very dark skies let them be spotted from Chile too. The debris travels in parallel, yet perspective makes the meteors seem to spread from one point in Perseus, low on the horizon here and partly hidden by the telescope enclosures. That radiant gives the shower its name.

understand.summary: This is one frame from continuous time-lapse photography with three cameras; the source gives no exposure settings.
understand.eye: A meteor lasts only a moment; the camera records its trail and the faint sky around it more fully than the eye could.

explore: According to the International Meteor Organization, the 2010 shower was above normal, peaking at over 100 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, but not spectacular. Many thousands of people watched worldwide, some for citizen science projects such as Meteorwatch.
alt: A bright meteor streaking over the VLT platform and enclosures, lit by reddish moonlight.
